chapter: History I · The Rise of Nationalism in Europe
source: NCERT India and the Contemporary World II (Class X History), Chapter I

overview.bigIdea: In 1789 the French Revolution gave Europe a new idea – **the people, not the king, make the nation**. Through the 19th century liberals, revolutionaries, artists and then conservative statesmen turned this idea into **nation-states**, until nationalism joined imperialism and led to war in 1914.

ladder.a: Liberal middle classes vs conservative Vienna order
Bismarck’s Germany, Cavour and Garibaldi’s Italy
Balkans and imperialism → First World War

lessons.title: The French Revolution and the idea of the nation
lessons.hook: In 1848 the French artist **Frédéric Sorrieu** drew the peoples of Europe and America marching past the statue of Liberty – each group with its own flag. His ‘utopian’ dream of a world of democratic nations started with France in **1789**.

core.def: A state in which the majority of citizens, not only rulers, share a sense of common identity and shared history or descent.

Ideas of la patrie (fatherland) and le citoyen (citizen); tricolour flag; Estates General renamed National Assembly; new hymns, oaths, martyrs; uniform laws; no internal customs; uniform weights and measures; French of Paris as common language.
Ended privileges based on birth, gave equality before the law and secured the right to property.
Simpler administrative divisions, end of feudal system, peasants freed from serfdom and manorial dues, guild restrictions removed, better transport and communication.
A nation is a large-scale solidarity built on a shared past and a common will – ‘a daily plebiscite’, not just language, race, religion or territory.

explain: **Mixed reactions:** in Holland, Switzerland, Brussels, Mainz, Milan and Warsaw the French were first welcomed as harbingers of liberty. Soon increased taxation, censorship and forced conscription outweighed the benefits.
**Absolutist vs modern:** Napoleon destroyed democracy in France by returning to monarchy, yet his administration followed revolutionary principles.

example.q: What steps did the French revolutionaries take to create a sense of collective identity among the French people? (3/5 marks)
steps: **Ideas:** la patrie and le citoyen stressed a united community with equal rights under a constitution.
**Symbols:** a new tricolour replaced the royal standard; new hymns, oaths and martyrs commemorated in the nation’s name.
**Institutions:** the Estates General was elected by active citizens and renamed the National Assembly.
**Uniform administration:** centralised system with uniform laws; internal customs duties abolished; uniform weights and measures.
**Language:** regional dialects discouraged; French of Paris became the common language.
example.answer: Ideas, symbols, assembly, uniform laws and economy, one language – five points.

mistakes: Saying Napoleon brought democracy (he restored monarchy).
Mixing up the Napoleonic Code (1804) with the Treaty of Vienna (1815).
Thinking all conquered people welcomed French rule throughout.
lessons.tip: For Napoleon questions write two columns: ‘Administrative gains’ and ‘What people disliked’ (taxes, censorship, conscription).
lessons.memory: 1789 Revolution · 1804 Code · Patrie + Citoyen · Flag, Assembly, Laws, Measures, Language.
examAsk: Steps taken by French revolutionaries to create collective identity.

lessons.title: Liberals, conservatives and revolutionaries
lessons.hook: Imagine paying customs duty **11 times** on one trip from Hamburg to Nuremberg, and the ‘elle’ of cloth being a different length in every town. No wonder the new middle class wanted **one nation, one market**.

core.def: Small but dominant landed class; spoke French in high society; linked by marriage across regions.
From liber (free): individual freedom, equality before law, government by consent, constitution and parliament, end of autocracy and clerical privilege, inviolable private property, free markets.
Customs union led by Prussia; abolished tariff barriers; cut currencies from over thirty to two; railways added mobility.
Preserve monarchy, Church, social hierarchies, property and family; prefer gradual change; use modernisation to strengthen monarchy.

Hosted by Metternich; Bourbons restored; buffer states around France (Netherlands incl. Belgium; Genoa added to Piedmont); Prussia gained western lands; Austria got northern Italy; Russia got part of Poland.
Born Genoa 1805; Carbonari member; exiled 1831; founded Young Italy (Marseilles) and Young Europe (Berne); wanted a unified Italian republic.

explain: **Limited suffrage:** in revolutionary France only property-owning men could vote; the Napoleonic Code reduced women to the status of a minor. Women and non-propertied men organised movements for equal political rights.
**After 1815:** conservative regimes were autocratic, used censorship and drove liberals underground into secret societies.

example.q: What did liberal nationalism stand for? (3 marks)
steps: **Politically:** freedom for the individual, equality before the law, government by consent – a constitution and representative government through parliament.
**Socially:** end of autocracy and clerical privileges; inviolability of private property.
**Economically:** freedom of markets and abolition of state restrictions on the movement of goods and capital – e.g. the Zollverein of 1834.
example.answer: Political, social and economic sides – with the Zollverein as the example.

mistakes: Saying liberals wanted universal suffrage – they mostly gave votes to property-owning men.
Saying the Treaty of Vienna broke up the German confederation (it was left untouched).
lessons.tip: Learn the Treaty of Vienna as ‘Restore + Contain’: restore monarchs (Bourbons) and contain France with buffer states.
lessons.memory: Liber = free · Zollverein 1834 (30 → 2 currencies) · Vienna 1815 (Metternich) · Mazzini: Young Italy, Young Europe.

lessons.title: The age of revolutions, 1830–1848
lessons.hook: ‘When France sneezes, the rest of Europe catches cold,’ said Metternich. In **1830** and again in **1848** France sneezed – and revolutions spread from Brussels to Frankfurt.

core.def: Bourbon kings overthrown in France; constitutional monarchy under Louis Philippe; Belgium breaks away from the United Kingdom of the Netherlands.
Began 1821 against the Ottoman Empire; supported by West Europeans like Lord Byron (died 1824); Treaty of Constantinople, 1832.
Culture over reason: emotions, folk songs, poetry, dances (Herder’s das volk, volksgeist); Grimm brothers’ folktales; Poland’s music and language (Kurpinski, polonaise, mazurka).
1830s: population boom, unemployment, slums, cheap English imports; 1845 Silesian weavers’ revolt; 1848 Paris – Louis Philippe flees, Republic with suffrage for men above 21.
831 representatives in the Church of St Paul; constitution with a monarchy subject to parliament; crown refused by Friedrich Wilhelm IV; disbanded by troops.

explain: **Women in 1848:** they formed associations and newspapers but were denied suffrage and admitted only as observers in the gallery of the Frankfurt parliament (compare Welcker and Otto-Peters in Source C).
**Result:** conservatives suppressed 1848 but could not restore the old order – serfdom and bonded labour were abolished in the Habsburg dominions and Russia; Hungarians got more autonomy in 1867.

example.q: Explain what is meant by the 1848 revolution of the liberals. (5 marks)
steps: **Who:** the educated middle classes, alongside revolts of the poor and unemployed.
**Where:** France (Republic with universal male suffrage) and regions without nation-states – Germany, Italy, Poland, Austria-Hungary.
**Demands:** a nation-state on parliamentary principles – a constitution, freedom of the press and freedom of association.
**Frankfurt:** 831 deputies drafted a constitution; Friedrich Wilhelm IV rejected the crown; troops disbanded the assembly.
**Limits and outcome:** women denied suffrage; middle class ignored workers; yet monarchs later granted concessions like abolishing serfdom.

mistakes: Confusing the 1830 July Revolution (Louis Philippe installed) with 1848 (Louis Philippe flees).
Forgetting that culture (Romanticism) also built nationalism, not only wars.
lessons.tip: For ‘role of culture’ questions give three examples: Romantic art (Delacroix), folk culture (Herder, Grimms), language/music in Poland.
lessons.memory: 1821 Greece starts · 1830 July Revolution · 1832 Greece free · 1845 Silesia · 1848 Paris & Frankfurt.
examAsk: Role of culture in the growth of nationalism in Europe.

lessons.title: The making of Germany, Italy and Britain
lessons.hook: Can the **army** be the architect of a nation? In Germany it was – Bismarck used ‘three wars over seven years’. In Italy a diplomat (Cavour) and a sailor-soldier (Garibaldi) did the job. Britain took centuries.

core.def: 1848 liberal attempt crushed by monarchy, military and Junkers; Prussia leads; Bismarck; wars with Austria, Denmark, France; William I proclaimed Emperor at Versailles, 18 January 1871.
Seven states – only Sardinia-Piedmont under an Italian princely house; north Austrian Habsburgs, centre the Pope, south Bourbon kings of Spain.

Mazzini’s 1831 and 1848 uprisings failed; Cavour’s alliance with France defeats Austria (1859); Garibaldi’s Red Shirts take the Two Sicilies (1860); Victor Emmanuel II king (1861); Papal States join 1870.
Long process; English parliament (1688); Act of Union 1707 with Scotland; Scottish Highlanders’ culture suppressed; Ireland incorporated 1801; Union Jack, anthem, English language promoted.

explain: **Prussian model:** the new German state modernised currency, banking, legal and judicial systems; Prussian practices became the model.
**Unaware masses:** southern peasants thought ‘La Talia’ was Victor Emmanuel’s wife – nationalism was an elite project.

example.q: Briefly trace the process of German unification. (5 marks)
steps: **1848:** middle-class Germans tried to unite the confederation under an elected parliament (Frankfurt).
**Repression:** the monarchy, military and Junkers crushed this liberal initiative.
**Prussia leads:** chief minister Otto von Bismarck with the Prussian army and bureaucracy.
**Three wars over seven years:** against Austria, Denmark and France – all Prussian victories.
**1871:** William I proclaimed German Emperor in the Hall of Mirrors, Versailles; Prussian measures became the model for Germany.

mistakes: Making Garibaldi the king of Italy.
Saying Germany was unified by the Frankfurt parliament.
Writing that Britain was formed by revolution.
lessons.tip: Italy = 3 people, 3 roles: Mazzini (ideas), Cavour (diplomacy), Garibaldi (volunteers) – and the king Victor Emmanuel II.
lessons.memory: Germany: Bismarck, 3 wars, 1871 Versailles · Italy: 1859, 1860, 1861, 1870 · Britain: 1688, 1707, 1801.
examAsk: Trace the process of German unification.

lessons.title: Visualising the nation; nationalism and imperialism
lessons.hook: How do you draw a **nation**? Artists made it a woman – **Marianne** for France, **Germania** for Germany. But by 1871 nationalism had turned narrow and aggressive.

core.def: An abstract idea expressed through a person or thing; nations shown as female figures not representing any real woman.
France; red cap, tricolour, cockade; statues in public squares; on coins and stamps.
Germany; crown of oak leaves (heroism); Veit’s 1848 banner hung in the Church of St Paul.
Broken chains – being freed; eagle breastplate – strength; oak crown – heroism; sword – readiness to fight; olive branch – peace; black-red-gold – liberal flag of 1848; rising sun – new era.
Romania, Bulgaria, Albania, Greece, Macedonia, Croatia, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Slovenia, Serbia, Montenegro – Slavs; Ottoman decline; big-power rivalry → wars and the First World War.

explain: **After 1871** nationalism lost its liberal-democratic idealism; groups became intolerant and ready for war; big powers manipulated subject peoples for imperialist aims.
**Colonies** developed anti-imperial nationalism of their own, but accepted the idea of the nation-state as universal.

example.q: Why did nationalist tensions emerge in the Balkans? (5 marks)
steps: **Diversity:** a region of geographical and ethnic variation whose people were broadly known as Slavs.
**Ottoman decline:** reforms failed; subject nationalities broke away one by one.
**Romantic nationalism:** people used history to claim long-lost independence.
**Rivalry among Balkan states:** each was jealous and wanted territory at the others’ expense.
**Big-power rivalry:** Russia, Germany, England and Austro-Hungary competed for control – a series of wars and finally the First World War.
example.answer: Diversity, Ottoman decline, romantic claims, mutual jealousy, big powers.

mistakes: Saying Marianne was a real French queen.
Mixing up the meanings of the sword and the olive branch.
Leaving out big-power rivalry in Balkans answers.
lessons.tip: For image questions: name the allegory, list 2–3 attributes from Box 3, then say what message they give together.
lessons.memory: Marianne = France (red cap) · Germania = Germany (oak = heroism) · Balkans = Slavs + Ottoman decline + big powers.
examAsk: Who were Marianne and Germania? Why were they portrayed this way?

revision: Sorrieu’s 1848 prints show a utopian world of democratic and social republics.
French Revolution (1789): la patrie, le citoyen, tricolour, National Assembly, uniform laws, weights and measures, French of Paris.
Napoleonic Code (1804): no privileges by birth, equality before law, right to property; feudalism and serfdom abolished in conquered areas.
French rule turned unpopular: taxes, censorship, forced conscription.
Liberalism (liber = free): individual freedom, equality before law, government by consent; free markets; but votes only for property-owning men.
Zollverein 1834: tariff barriers abolished, currencies from over 30 to 2.
Treaty of Vienna 1815 (Metternich): Bourbons restored; Netherlands incl. Belgium; Austria gets northern Italy; German confederation of 39 states untouched.
Mazzini: Carbonari, Young Italy, Young Europe – ‘most dangerous enemy of our social order’.
1830 July Revolution; Belgium breaks away; Greece independent by Treaty of Constantinople 1832.
Romanticism: Delacroix, Herder’s das volk, Grimm brothers, Polish language and music.
1848: Paris Republic with male suffrage; Frankfurt parliament (831 deputies, St Paul’s) fails; women only observers.
Germany 1871: Bismarck, three wars, William I at Versailles.
Italy: Cavour + France beat Austria 1859; Garibaldi 1860; Victor Emmanuel II 1861; Rome 1870.
Britain: long process – 1688, 1707, 1801; English culture dominant.
Marianne and Germania are allegories; Balkans were the powder keg before 1914.

sections.title: Unification answers · 4 steps
items: State the starting situation (divided states, who ruled them).
Name the leaders and their roles.
Give the events in date order.
End with the result and its nature (e.g. ‘dominance of Prussian state power’).

sections.title: Answer writing that scores
items: Start with a one-line introduction using the textbook’s key term (e.g. ‘Proto-industrialisation was …’).
Write in points – one idea per point, key term first. A 3-mark answer needs 3 clear points; a 5-mark answer needs 5.
Add a date, a name or a figure from the chapter to each point – but only when you are sure of it.
For ‘Explain / Analyse’ use PEE: Point → Explain → Example. For ‘Compare’ draw a small two-column table.
Source-based questions: underline the key line in the source first; the answer is usually hidden in it.

sections.title: Before the exam
items: Revise the key facts sheet and the revision list the night before.
Redo the Play & learn timelines and sorts – if you get every card first time, you know the chapter.
Practise one 5-mark answer in 8–10 minutes with a timer.

checklist: I can list the French measures that created a collective identity.
I can explain Napoleon’s reforms and why people resented French rule.
I can explain liberalism, conservatism and the Treaty of Vienna.
I can describe 1830–1848, including Romanticism and the Frankfurt parliament.
I can trace German and Italian unification and explain Britain’s case.
I can interpret Marianne, Germania and the Balkan problem.
exam.paperNote: Based on the CBSE Class X Social Science pattern (MCQ, assertion–reason, 3-mark short, 4-mark source-based and 5-mark long answers; History also has map work). Practise these types first.

method: Built on proven learning methods: understand the story first, sort and match ideas with your hands (active learning), write model answers point by point, test yourself (active recall) and revisit after 1, 3 and 7 days (spaced revision).
